Summary: A 30‑year‑old woman with migraine with visual aura and combined oral contraceptive use experienced a five‑minute episode of painless left‑eye inferior visual field loss without headache or other focal signs. During the event a colleague captured retinal photographs that show a small intravascular retinal embolus with superior macular whitening; subsequent images demonstrate distal movement of the embolus and progressive fading of the whitening, correlating with symptom resolution. Examination after resolution is neurologically normal. Brain MRI, carotid and cardiac imaging, and shunt study are pending.

Why resolution and migraine history do not exclude a vascular cause: Transient monocular visual loss can be the first manifestation of retinal artery embolism, and migraine aura can mimic but does not produce a visible intravascular particle. The documented embolus and its dynamic retinal changes indicate a true embolic phenomenon rather than a purely migrainous aura, so the event cannot be attributed to migraine alone.

Urgency and assessment plan: Because an embolic source may recur and cause permanent infarction, urgent evaluation is warranted. Priority investigations include carotid duplex or CTA, transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography, prolonged cardiac rhythm monitoring, hypercoagulable laboratory panel, and assessment of oral contraceptive risk. The retinal findings confirm an embolic event; the embolic source remains unconfirmed and must be identified before any therapeutic decision.
